scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi IT!! The campus network keeps going SLOW in bursts.
People here say it might be router0, but I don't know if that is right.
Something around the main router box must be overloaded. Could someone look at
router0 and make the network stop crawling!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — intermittent network slowness attributed to router0 being overloaded — is unconfirmed by any live evidence.

A full four-phase sweep was conducted. Phase A (L2/infrastructure): `infra_sweep` found zero ACL rules, zero addressing anomalies, zero resolver divergence, and zero static ARP entries across all 30 devices. `l2_snapshot` showed only normal Linux kernel tunnel interfaces (tunl0, gre0, sit0, etc.) with all-zero MACs, which is baseline behaviour for containerised hosts — not a MAC conflict. Phase B (control plane and traffic shaping): `tc_snapshot` confirmed every interface in the topology uses the default `pfifo_fast` qdisc with no shaping, limiting, or netem injection whatsoever. RIP v2 is the routing protocol; all three routers have fully converged tables with correct routes to all subnets and no rejected or backup entries. Phase D (resource pressure): `pressure_sweep` found no stress tools, flood processes, or CPU or socket pressure on any device, including router0. Router0's startup script contains only standard interface-address and RIP-daemon configuration — no periodic tc injection or load-generation commands. Interface counters on router0 show startup-level packet counts (16 RX / 15 TX on the WAN link) and zero errors, drops, FIFO overruns, or carrier events. There is no flap script, no cron job, and no historical trace of the claimed slowness. The current network state is fully healthy with 0% packet loss and sub-5 ms RTT across all sampled paths. The claim is unconfirmed.

per_axis.rationale: The report confirms 0% loss and healthy interface counters but does not explicitly state that router0's ip_forward is enabled.

The agent's investigation log shows reachability tests with 0% loss, qdisc/TC clean, routing converged, no pressure or stress processes, and zero interface errors on router0 — the writeup's claims are grounded and the conclusion (no anomaly) follows logically. One minor omission is an explicit sysctl ip_forward check, but successful end-to-end pings and routing evidence adequately demonstrate forwarding is working.
